name: Charlie Bird’s Farro Salad
headnote: A farro salad from the SoHo restaurant Charlie Bird, adapted by Melissa Clark from chef Ryan Hardy. The trick is seasoning the grain itself: the farro simmers in apple cider with bay leaves and a good deal of salt so it tastes good before anything is added. It is then enriched with generous olive oil, pistachios and Parmesan, and finished with tomatoes, radishes, arugula and herbs folded in just before serving.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (979) explains the recipe's biggest variable: pearled versus unpearled farro cook at very different rates, so go by texture rather than the stated time. A 692-vote note used Trader Joe's 10-minute farro with 1 cup cider plus 1 cup water and simmered only about 15 minutes. Several cooks (579 votes) improvise the cider with roughly 1/2 to 3/4 cup apple cider vinegar plus 1 to 2 tablespoons honey topped up with water, though another popular note (469) warns readers not to confuse cider with cider vinegar in the cooking liquid itself. A repeated complaint (542 votes) is that the salt in the farro is too much once salty Parmesan goes on top; cut it back. Roasted vegetables are a common addition.

name: Classic Meat Tortellini with Tomato Sauce
headnote: A from-scratch tortellini project based on the version codified by Bologna's Confraternita del Tortellino, with the usual legend about the shape echoing Venus's navel. Traditionally these are served in a light meat broth, but here they are tossed with a simple tomato sauce and a little Parmesan as a main course. The yield is generous, and both pasta and sauce freeze well separately.
comment_digest: Only a handful of notes, and the loudest theme is time: the top comment flatly says to budget about three hours rather than the listed hour and fifteen minutes, and a second cook makes the same complaint while calling the method overcomplicated. Both still count the tomato sauce a success. Two separate cooks disliked the filling for the same reason, describing it as crumbly, dry and off-putting in texture; one said the leftover pasta scraps tasted better than the finished tortellini, and another praised the red sauce while conceding the filling may be a matter of personal taste. Nobody offered a fix for the filling.

name: Classic Pasta Alla Norma
headnote: A plain, traditional Sicilian dish built on four cheap staples: olive oil, eggplant, tomato and pasta, finished with grated ricotta salata and toasted bread crumbs. The name is popularly traced to Bellini's opera and the composer's fondness for the dish.
comment_digest: The top note (140 votes) argues for an ordering change: toss the pasta with the tomato sauce first and add the eggplant afterward, otherwise the eggplant flavour disappears into the sauce. The next most-voted tip (67) is that the frying oil must be up to temperature before the eggplant goes in, or the cubes soak it up. A large contingent skips frying entirely: broiling or roasting the eggplant comes up repeatedly (49 and 31 votes), with cooks saying they lose no flavour and use far less oil, and one warning that roasted eggplant vanishes off the sheet pan before it reaches the pot. A Sicilian-heritage commenter offers context on the dish's name. Garlic quantity is treated as a floor, not a ceiling.

name: Cold Noodle Salad with Spicy Peanut Sauce
headnote: Cold soba noodles tossed with a spicy peanut sauce and a heap of raw crunchy vegetables, with the vegetables treated as fully swappable (cabbage, carrot, fennel, asparagus, broccoli, cauliflower). Any nut or seed butter can stand in for the peanut butter, including tahini. Noodles and sauce can both be made a day ahead but should be combined only at serving, and the sauce needs a spoonful or two of water to loosen after it sits.
comment_digest: Peanut butter choice dominates. The highest-voted note (1,238) explains that conventional emulsified peanut butters blend into the sauce more readily than natural ones because of the added oils, and a 797-vote note raises the same natural-versus-processed question; a 638-vote commenter recommends powdered peanut butter reconstituted with water for a lower-fat sauce, warning about added sugar in some brands. On technique, a 555-vote note says to stop whisking by hand and instead use an immersion blender in a deep measuring cup with about 1/4 cup water. A 687-vote tip changes assembly: dress the noodles with sauce first and lay the vegetables on top so they stay crisp and keep their colour. Fresh ginger and cilantro in the sauce, and sriracha for the chile oil, are common additions.

name: Creamed Spinach Pasta
headnote: Colu Henry's weeknight pasta borrows from the steakhouse side dish. A full pound of fresh spinach wilts down in garlicky butter, cream goes in and simmers until thick, and the cooked pasta finishes in the sauce with ricotta stirred through. Long noodles such as fettuccine or tagliatelle hold the sauce best. Nuts on top are optional, and it works either as a side to grilled meat or fish or as a meal on its own.
comment_digest: The highest-voted note (263) says ricotta quality decides the texture: good whole-milk ricotta keeps the sauce smooth, yogurt is a passable substitute and cottage cheese was judged a poor one, though a 158-vote commenter disagrees and likes cottage cheese, while also calling the separate bowl for seasoning the ricotta a pointless extra dish. A 216-vote note skips fresh spinach entirely for two 16-ounce bags of frozen chopped spinach, microwaved and squeezed dry. Timing is the common correction (197 votes): a pound of fresh spinach takes well over the four minutes given. Cooks add lemon zest and juice at the end for brightness (168), and a 128-vote note reports the recipe works with any cooking green and with half-and-half in place of heavy cream.

name: Creamy Corn Pasta with Basil
headnote: Melissa Clark's summer pasta gets its creaminess from pureed fresh corn and sauteed scallions rather than any dairy cream, with Parmesan for savor and red chile flakes for contrast. Lemon juice and fresh herbs go in at the very end and matter, cutting the richness. Best at peak corn season, but the recipe is forgiving enough for supermarket ears or frozen kernels.
comment_digest: The dominant tip by a wide margin (900 votes) is to simmer the stripped cobs in water for 10 to 15 minutes and cook the pasta in that corn stock for deeper flavour, while holding back a larger share of whole kernels for texture. Adding halved or quartered grape tomatoes at the end for acidity is the next most popular change (410 votes), and shrimp with a clove of garlic and mint appears at 202 votes; bacon is a recurring suggestion. The main dissent is about sweetness: a 169-vote commenter who followed the recipe exactly found the corn puree cloying even after cheese, lemon and basil, and a 154-vote note calls the dish underwhelming for the effort. Chile flakes and lemon are the usual correctives.

name: Creamy Winter Squash Soup with Brown Butter Streusel Topping
headnote: A Wall Street Journal Slow Food Fast column featuring Anne Quatrano, the Atlanta chef behind Bacchanalia and several other restaurants, where the recipe first appeared more than a decade ago. Butternut squash is enriched with a little maple syrup and heavy cream and warmed with ginger and nutmeg. The garnish is a brown-butter streusel of toasted oats and pumpkin seeds, which Quatrano wants for the crunch against the velvety soup. She notes the dish is forgiving because squash is essentially impossible to overcook.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: WSJ article, no ratings or reader comments on the page

name: Crisp Gnocchi with Brussels Sprouts and Brown Butter
headnote: A 20-minute skillet dish built on one trick: store-bought gnocchi are never boiled, just seared until crisp and golden outside while staying chewy inside, closer to fried dough than to boiled dumplings. They are tossed with sauteed brussels sprouts, lemon zest, red-pepper flakes and brown butter. Both shelf-stable and refrigerated gnocchi work, though the shelf-stable kind crisps better.
comment_digest: The single loudest practical complaint concerns the sprouts: a 570-vote note reports they were nowhere near done in the stated five minutes, and the most-endorsed workaround is to roast them separately and fold them in. Several highly rated notes describe this (885, 678 and 597 votes), roasting at 425 to 450 degrees for 15 to 25 minutes while the gnocchi crisp on the stovetop, which keeps the total time close to 20 minutes and produces crispier sprouts; shallot and garlic are often added at the toss. A 1,551-vote note swaps a splash of aged balsamic for the honey, gaining acidity along with sweetness, and a 1,258-vote note confirms Trader Joe's cauliflower gnocchi works. The top comment by votes is an anecdote about the skillet in the photograph, not cooking advice.

name: Cumin-Baked Pork Chops
headnote: A quick pork chop recipe that reached The Times in 1997 through Molly O'Neill's feature on cumin. The chops are coated and baked, and the recipe suggests crushing whole cumin seeds rather than using pre-ground for a bit of fresh texture, while allowing ground cumin as a substitute.
comment_digest: Toughness is the recurring problem and brining is the top-voted fix (240 votes): about 45 minutes in roughly 3 tablespoons table salt per quart of water, then rinse, before proceeding. Several of the next most helpful notes rearrange the order of operations, since cooks report the mustard coating makes browning difficult: brown the chops first in a little oil for about 2 minutes a side, let them cool slightly, then apply the Dijon and crushed cumin before the oven (216 and 116 votes). A 216-vote cook used thick 1 1/4-inch bone-in chops and worked about 3/4 teaspoon ground cumin into the mustard. Ground cumin mixed straight into the mustard works fine (93 votes), a nonstick skillet prevents sticking with 10 minutes in the oven right for 8-ounce chops (69), and one cook skipped the searing entirely and still liked it.

name: Curried Chicken Breast with Zucchini
headnote: A Pierre Franey 60-Minute Gourmet weeknight skillet dish. Boneless chicken breasts (thighs work too) and zucchini are tossed with curry powder, oil, salt and pepper and browned, then the pan is emptied and a fast sauce built from shallots, chicken broth, heavy cream, oil and butter; everything goes back in to warm through. Serve over rice, couscous or with mashed potatoes.
comment_digest: The top note (295 votes) lists three worthwhile changes: fresh ginger with the shallots, dropping the butter and relying on pan juices, and a substitution for the cream. Doubling the sauce is a short, emphatic recommendation (65 votes) on the grounds that the sauce is what makes the dish. Coconut milk in place of heavy cream comes up more than once, served with couscous and cucumber raita, and a 54-vote cook added sweet potatoes and suggests mushrooms would work. One cook substituted vermouth when broth was not to hand. Cooks are generally heavy-handed with the curry powder and say they would go further; thick breasts need somewhat longer than the stated time. A 184-vote note is a fond reminiscence about Franey rather than a cooking tip.

name: Dry-Brined Turkey
headnote: A Thanksgiving turkey that applies Judy Rodgers's Zuni Cafe method of salting birds well in advance instead of soaking them in liquid brine, which the recipe argues changes the texture of the meat. The payoff is crisp golden skin over moist meat. The bird needs two days in the refrigerator to season before it is roasted.
comment_digest: The most-voted comment by a wide margin (1,692) is a challenge to the method rather than a report: if the point is to dry the skin, why wrap the bird in plastic in the fridge? A 701-vote note raises the same question from the air-drying angle, and many cooks resolve it by leaving the bird uncovered for the final stretch. A 253-vote note answers a common worry: after two days there is no salt left to rinse off because it has dissolved into the meat, so just blot the surface dry with paper towels. A 337-vote question about whether the bird can be stuffed under this method, and how to adjust the 12-minutes-per-pound guideline, goes largely unresolved. Among people reporting results, a 292-vote cook called it the best turkey they had made and confirmed 1/2 cup salt was right. Convection roasting is discussed.
flags: top comments are questions rather than tested corrections

name: Einkorn Risotto with Fresh Herbs
headnote: A straightforward risotto made with einkorn rather than rice, flavoured with shallots, optional garlic and a generous quantity of marjoram, chives and parsley. The herbs carry enough flavour that the Parmesan finish can be left out, making it workable as a vegan main or side.
comment_digest: There are only a few notes and none of them report actually cooking the dish, so there is no tested guidance on liquid, timing or texture. The entire discussion is about the grain itself: several readers ask what einkorn is and where to buy it, and the answers identify it as an ancient variety of wheat domesticated roughly 11,000 years ago, sold as einkorn wheat berries, stocked by health food stores and Whole Foods and available fresh at the Union Square Greenmarket in New York. One commenter notes that einkorn does contain gluten despite its reputation as a health grain, and suggests spelt or farro as workable substitutes in this recipe.
flags: only 3 notes, none from cooks who made it; one extraction call was blocked by a URL in a comment

name: Farro Salad with Beets, Greens and Feta
headnote: Farro is sturdy and nutty enough to carry assertive partners like beets, their greens and salty feta, and the grain turns it into a main course; poached or roasted chicken is suggested if more substance is wanted. The red beets tint the farro pink, and the colour deepens over hours, so the salad can be assembled a day ahead and travels well for picnics. The instruction that matters most is to soak the grain for an hour and cook it until genuinely tender, or the result is chewy.
comment_digest: The clearest gap cooks point out (74 votes) is that the headnote refers to roasted beets while the recipe steps never say to roast them, leaving the beet method to the cook. Many answer that themselves by avoiding the oven: a 35-vote note pressure-cooked golden beets for 15 to 30 minutes on high rather than roasting in July, and another popular note used a comparable stovetop shortcut. Goat cheese is confirmed as an equal substitute for feta (82 votes), and a 45-vote cook rebuilt the dish gluten-free with Lentils du Puy in place of farro plus lightly steamed lacinato kale, parsley and chives. A 57-vote note says the oil quantity is too high. Carrots and radishes are common additions.

name: Fast French Onion Soup
headnote: A Washington Post version of the classic that borrows J. Kenji Lopez-Alt's shortcut for caramelizing onions: sugar, baking soda and higher heat to compress what is normally a long process. The Post's testers rated it the richest of the several versions they tried, dark enough to pass for homemade beef broth even though it is built on store-bought chicken broth. If the serving bowls are not broiler-safe, the cheese-topped bread can be broiled separately on a sheet pan and floated on top. A published correction notes the recipe originally called for baking powder; both work, but soda caramelizes faster.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: Washington Post page, headnote only, no reader comments or rating

name: Fettuccine Alfredo — Elaine’s
headnote: Alex Witchel brought this to The Times in a 2004 piece on Elaine Kaufman, whose Manhattan restaurant served it to a famous clientele. The recipe makes no claim to refinement and is described as upmarket macaroni and cheese, rich and satisfying rather than clever.
comment_digest: The highest-voted notes are not cooking advice but a long argument about authenticity: a 1,685-vote comment points out that the dish is Elaine's own version, not an attempt at a canonical Roman alfredo, and two more of the top notes (1,020 and 884 votes) tell readers to stop bickering and cook what their household will eat. The most useful practical note (331 votes) warns that the sauce can break unless you are confident, and recommends cream cheese with milk in place of cream as a more forgiving base. A 357-vote commenter argues against fat-free half-and-half on the grounds of what is added to it, and a 299-vote cook adds peas. Overall the comments are light on tested technique beyond the splitting problem.
flags: top-voted comments are debate rather than technique

name: Fettuccine with Asparagus and Smoked Salmon
headnote: A quick, slightly dressy pasta from a Times column on vegetables and pasta: fettuccine, asparagus and smoked salmon bound in a shallot cream sauce, done in well under an hour.
comment_digest: The top note by a clear margin (408 votes) saves a pan by dropping the asparagus into the pasta water for the last two minutes of cooking rather than boiling it separately, and suggests spring onion alongside or instead of the dill; a 90-vote cook confirms this works and says the cold-water shock can be skipped too. A 320-vote cook instead sautes the asparagus with the butter and shallots and reports success with squid-ink linguine and canned smoked salmon. Another practical tip (57 votes) is to skip peeling the stalks and simply steam the thicker end pieces briefly before adding the tips. A 102-vote note drops the cream entirely for a shallot-and-dill olive oil and still rates it highly. One cook found the sauce thinner than expected.

name: Fettuccine with Sausage and Fried Sage
headnote: From a 1997 Moira Hodgson piece arguing that sage deserves more than a Thanksgiving role. Frying the leaves in oil or butter, as Italians do, softens their strong earthy character to a trace. The crisped leaves come out of the pan, then a pound of hot Italian sausage and garlic brown in the flavoured oil, cream deglazes the pan, and the whole thing is tossed with fettuccine and Parmesan with the sage scattered over. About 30 minutes.
comment_digest: A small comment set with modest vote counts. The most-endorsed change (29 votes) is to squeeze the sausage out of its casings and crumble it while frying rather than cutting it into chunks, and a related tip (12 votes) is to slit the casings lengthwise while the sausages are still very cold from thawing, which makes them come away cleanly. Quantity is the other recurring note (14 votes): the sauce as written barely coats a full pound of fettuccine, so either increase the cream or use less pasta. One cook found the dish bland made as written and plans considerably more garlic plus red-pepper flakes next time. Dried sage sprinkled into the oil is reported as an acceptable fallback when fresh is unavailable.

name: Fish Tacos
headnote: Sam Sifton's Baja-style fish tacos: fish fried in strips, served on warm corn tortillas with a simple salsa, shredded cabbage, plenty of lime and a cream sauce that can be sharpened with chopped chipotle. The recipe presents itself as no harder than making burgers. Sifton developed it after working with a chef who specialises in fish, and drew on the version at El Siete Mares on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, which closed in 2020.
comment_digest: The top note by a wide margin (1,063 votes) skips frying altogether: brush the fish strips with oil, roll them lightly in panko and bake at 400 degrees. A 420-vote cook does something similar with tilapia, brushing with olive oil and chipotle and baking about 12 minutes at 350. Greek yogurt in place of sour cream in the chipotle sauce is a popular and well-liked substitution (596 votes), and the sauce draws more praise than any other component. A 337-vote note from Ensenada, Baja California adds a traditional garnish: sliced onion marinated 24 hours in olive oil with a teaspoon of dried oregano. Several cooks (270 votes) treat the recipe as a build-your-own buffet with assorted tortillas and toppings, and multiple notes warn the prep chopping takes real time.

name: Fluffy Mashed Potatoes
headnote: The method here rests on two choices: Russet Burbank baking potatoes, which mash without turning gluey, and steaming rather than boiling, so the potatoes are not waterlogged and keep their faintly sweet flavour. Seasoning is held to the very end for the same reason. A ricer is recommended for the smoothest texture, pressing the steamed potatoes straight back into the pot before butter and milk are folded in gently.
comment_digest: Make-ahead reheating dominates the notes, starting with the most-voted comment (309) asking how to do it. The two best answers follow: a 229-vote note bakes them in the oven after pricking the surface with a fork and dotting with butter, and a 196-vote catering trick spreads them in an ovenproof dish, pours cream over, covers with foil and warms at 300 degrees until hot. A 59-vote cook reheats in a crockpot and says it has never failed over several Thanksgivings. The main challenge to the method is a 147-vote note preferring an Instant Pot, pressure cooking peeled chunks for 4 to 5 minutes on a steamer insert so they never sit in water. Folding finely grated Gruyere into the finished potatoes is a well-liked addition (108).

name: Free-Form Apple or Pear Tart
headnote: A Mark Bittman Minimalist recipe from a column on entertaining simply, for a rustic free-form tart made with either apples or pears. The page carries no descriptive headnote beyond the article credit, so the method itself is the whole story.
comment_digest: Handling the dough is what cooks talk about. The top note (99 votes) says to roll it directly on parchment and slide the paper onto the baking sheet, removing any transfer anxiety; a 64-vote cook rolls it out on a baking stone instead, and a 32-vote note reports the dough is soft enough to simply pat out on the sheet pan with no rolling pin or parchment at all. Several cooks call the crust the best part, describing it as buttery and shortbread-like. Popular flavour changes (23 votes) are cinnamon, nutmeg and cardamom sprinkled over the fruit and turbinado sugar in place of brown. Ripe pears, including a glut of gift pears, are praised as well as apples, and one cook rested the dough a full 24 hours in the fridge with good results.
flags: page has no real headnote, only a 'Featured in' credit

name: French Yogurt Cake with Marmalade Glaze
headnote: Emily Weinstein's note frames this as a deliberately plain, faintly tangy everyday cake, served in France with lightly sweetened creme fraiche. Because it is unassertive it takes almost any accompaniment: sliced peaches or plums, sugared berries, lemon curd or mousse, or chocolate mousse or sauce.
comment_digest: The recipe's own wording is the main complaint. A 94-vote note points out that step 3 refers to a round pan without ever giving a size, and a 71-vote note finds the pan and timing instructions contradictory, since one step specifies an 8 1/2-by-4 1/2-inch loaf pan while the times cover both a round cake (35 to 40 minutes) and a loaf (50 to 55). An 8-by-8 square pan is reported to work. The most-voted note (170) comes from a repeat baker who cut the oil to 1/3 cup and swaps sour cream or creme fraiche for the yogurt. A 104-vote request for a butter-for-oil conversion is answered at 70 votes with Amanda Hesser's ratio of about 3/4 cup oil to 1 cup butter. Several cooks reduce the sugar to 1/2 cup.

name: Fruit Galette
headnote: Melissa Clark's template galette, written to work with whatever fruit is around; the variable to adjust is the sugar and cornstarch. Tart stone fruit such as apricots, peaches, nectarines, plums and sour cherries needs more of both, while figs, grapes, berries and Bing cherries need less, and she advises adding sugar gradually and tasting. A thin layer of jam under the fruit deepens the flavour, matched or contrasted as you like, and vanilla seeds, ground spices or minced candied ginger can replace the lemon zest. The dough holds three days, but the galette is best the day it is baked.
comment_digest: Leaking juice is the problem cooks hit, and the top note (445 votes) describes liquid escaping and burning on the sheet pan; the fix borrowed from the NYT blueberry pie is to drain the macerated fruit and use that liquid separately. An 81-vote note asks for an explicit warning about how much liquid berries release, raspberries especially. The second most-voted tip (215) is a genuine ambiguity in the instructions: do not pour the whole egg-and-cream mixture onto the crust, which the recipe only makes clear too late. A 115-vote note recommends watching the accompanying video for technique, and cooks endorse making the crust in a food processor (98 votes). Popular additions are cardamom or cinnamon with peaches, and lime with mango.
